newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: Daewoo hopes set back by French government.
newsitem.headline: Daewoo hopes set back by French government.

text.p: Hopes of South Korea's Daewoo to escape domestic woes and become a global electronics leader have been dealt a blow by a French decision to put off selling Thomson SA, analysts said on Thursday.
Some Korean analysts saw the French government move as racist, while the chairman of Daewoo Electronics said he wanted the "real reason" behind the shock announcement on Wednesday.

The purchase of state-owned Thomson Multimedia would have transformed Daewoo Electronics from a relatively unknown Asian corporation, struggling to maintain market share at home, into the world's biggest television maker with established brand names and leading edge technology.
"Thomson would have given it a shot at the big league," said Stephen Marvin, head of research at Ssangyong Investment and Securities Co Ltd.
"We've concluded that the deal will take longer than expected, at best, but more likely will be scuttled."
The French government said the suspension of the proposed Thomson sell-off to Lagardere Groupe was because of objections to the sale of its giant consumer electronics division to Daewoo.

"We are trying to find out the real reason behind the French government's announcement of temporarily suspending the privatisation process," a Daewoo Electronics spokesman quoted chairman Bae Soon-hoon as saying.
"We'll closely examine and confront any development to the situation," the Daewoo chairman added.
A Daewoo statement said the move was "unexpected and regretful".
Bae had offered to create 5,000 new jobs at Thomson within five years to try to win over sceptical labour unions. But the unions never warmed to the idea of South Koreans taking over.
"This is a racist decision," said Tony Jung, an electronics analyst at Jardine Fleming Securities.

"The French couldn't accept the fact that Thomson Multimedia was being taken over by a company from a small country in the East. It was hurting their pride. It could have been different if Thomson was taken over by an American company."
South Korean companies in Asia have a reputation for tough, and occasionally brutal, management.
"Day-to-day management would have been a bit more authoritarian than French workers are used to," said Marvin.

Daewoo is being elbowed aside in its home markets by powerful competitors Samsung Electronics and LG Electronics, and was looking to Thomson to give it a boost with huge economies of scale, brokers said.
Thomson also offered brand recognition that Daewoo lacked to compete against Japanese products.
And Thomson had an inside track on the vast American market about to open in high definition television (HDTV) as part of a consortium setting industry standards.
Marvin said Daewoo, encouraged by the South Korean government, made a grab for Thomson partly for its potential to set technology standards.
"It scared the hell out of the Japanese," he said.
Other analysts argued that the Thomson deal never made sense for Daewoo.
"Daewoo is already terribly over-leveraged and losing ground domestically to LG and Samsung," said Matt Cleary, a Seoul-based electronics analyst with HG Asia Ltd.
"I saw this move as one of desperation all along. It just seemed like they had to do something dramatic while they still had the energy to do it."
Analysts said losing the Thomson deal would delay but certainly not halt Daewoo's charge offshore.
"Daewoo will try to take over another high-profile company if the Thomson takeover fails," said Jung of Jardine Fleming.
